title: Signature of Short-Range Order in Static Response of the Three-Dimensional Electron Gas
authors: Muhammed H. Güneş, Yubo Yang, Vitaly Gorelov, Miguel A. Morales, Matteo Gatti, Lucia Reining, Shiwei Zhang
abstract: The three-dimensional electron gas is a fundamental model in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry, and the exchange-correlation energy derived from it serves as the starting point of \textit{ab initio} computations of materials. However, the wave-vector-dependent response, and hence the static local field factor $G(q)$, has remained without accurate ground-state benchmark in the strongly coupled regime for three decades. Using diffusion Monte Carlo, we calculate $G(q)$ and the static density-density response function across the liquid phase and find a pronounced structure in $G(q)$ at intermediate wave vectors, already visible at metallic densities and growing with increasing interaction strength. We identify it as a fingerprint of short-range order by showing that it is required to reproduce the static structure factor. Our parametrization, valid in the entire liquid phase, predicts a low-energy resonant mode inside the particle-hole continuum.
summary: This work uses Diffusion Monte Carlo simulations to calculate the static response functions of the 3D electron gas in the strongly coupled regime. The authors identify a distinct structural feature in the local field factor G(q) at intermediate wave vectors. This feature is argued to be a direct signature of short-range order, providing a crucial benchmark for understanding electronic correlations beyond simple approximations.
main_problem: The study aims to accurately determine the wave-vector-dependent static local field factor G(q) and the static density-density response function for the 3D electron gas, particularly in the strongly coupled (low-density) regime.
main_result: The calculations reveal a pronounced, non-trivial structure in G(q) at intermediate wave vectors, which is identified as a fingerprint of short-range order and is necessary to correctly reproduce the static structure factor.
method: The primary method involves using Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) simulations to calculate the response functions, which are then analyzed using theoretical parametrizations.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the three-dimensional electron gas (HEG), a fundamental model in condensed matter physics used as a starting point for ab initio calculations of materials.
key_observables: Static local field factor G(q), static density-density response function $\chi(q)$, and the static structure factor $S(q)$.
important_parameters: The Wigner-Seitz radius ($r_s$), which controls the coupling strength, is varied across the strongly coupled regime ($r_s > 10$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on DMC calculations for benchmark data and utilizes the Single-Mode Approximation (SMA) for certain derived quantities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate G(q) vs $r_s$ showing the structural feature, the exchange-correlation kernel $f_{	ext{xc}}(r)$ confirming real-space structure, and $\chi(q)$ and $S(q)$ showing the correlated structure.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem, presents DMC calculations of $\chi(q)$ and $G(q)$ across various densities, identifies the structural feature in $G(q)$ required by $S(q)$, and discusses the implications for low-energy resonant modes.
why_interesting: The study provides benchmark data on electronic correlations in a fundamental model, which is crucial for developing accurate theoretical inputs for many-body calculations relevant to correlated materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Local field factor G(q) of the electron gas for (a)–(e) rs = 5, 30, 50, 70, and 100. DMC data are shown as circles, obtained with Ne = 54 electrons, except for rs = 70, where Ne = 162. The solid line is our fit defined in Eq. (2), and dashdotted line is the analytical parametrization extrapolated by Ref. [24]. Dashed lines represent the low- and high-q limits.

FIG. 2. Exchange-correlation kernel fxc at rs = 90. The solid line is obtained from our fitted G(q), while the dashed line is obtained by manually removing the feature from the solid curve. Panel (a) shows fxc as a function of wave vector, while panel (c) shows the difference between the solid and dashed lines in (a). Panels (b) and (d) are the Fourier trans- forms of (a) and (c), respectively.

FIG. 3. (a) Static density response function χ(q) of the elec- tron gas for rs = 20–100 calculated from the analytical fit to our DMC data [Eq. (2)]. The dashed line shows the non- interacting response χ0(q). (b) The ratio χ(q)/χ0(q) of the curves in (a). (c) Static structure factor S(q) at rs = 100. Circles: direct computation (via equal-time pair correlation from separate DMC with Ne = 250), solid and dash-dotted lines: SMA results obtained through our χ(q) and the Cor- radini et al. parametrization, respectively. In all panels, the black arrows mark the first and second peak positions; red arrows mark the midpoint between the peaks. SMA results are scaled for better visibility.

FIG. 4. (a) Dynamic structure factor S(q, ω) for rs = 90 calculated using the static G(q) as the xc kernel in the linear- response χ(q, ω). Solid orange line: collective mode dispersion from the peak of S(q, ω). Dashed line: the non-interacting dis- persion, ω0q = q2/2. Data points: collective mode dispersion using DMC S(q) as input for SMA, i.e. ωq = q2/[2S(q)]. (b) The solid orange line in (a) divided by ω0q. The white and red arrows mark the dips and peaks, respectively.
